The proposed answer of 355 is wrong. The correct minimum is **499**.

**Where the proposed solution goes wrong.** Its construction is valid, with \(S_1=\{1\}\), \(S_2=\{2\}\), \(S_5=\{3,\dots,6\}\), \(S_{10}=\{7,\dots,10\}\), \(S_{25}=\{11,\dots,30\}\), \(S_{50}=\{31,\dots,50\}\), \(S_{125}=\{51,\dots,150\}\), \(S_{250}=\{151,\dots,250\}\). But the table in §8 omits each block's own maximum for \(d=10, 50, 125\). Since \(A_d\) contains \(S_d\), the correct values are:

| \(d\) | \(\max A_d\) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 |
| 5 | 6 |
| 10 | 10 |
| 25 | 30 |
| 50 | 50 |
| 125 | 150 |
| 250 | 250 |

This sums to \(499\), not \(355\).

**Why 499 is optimal.** Write \(T_d=\max A_d\) and \(x=T_{50}\), \(y=T_{125}\).

- The structure \(A_e=\bigsqcup_{d\mid e}S_d\) with \(|S_d|=\varphi(d)\) and disjoint \(S_d\) is forced, and any such family works, so the problem reduces to placing these blocks.
- \(T_{250}\ge 250\), since the 250 elements of the eight blocks are distinct positive integers.
- \(T_1+T_2+T_5\ge 9\): if \(T_5=5\) then \(T_2\ge 6\) (sum \(\ge 12\)); otherwise \(T_5\ge 6\) and \(T_1+T_2+T_5\ge 1+2+6\).
- \(T_{10}+T_{25}\ge 40\): the 20 elements of \(S_{25}\) lie in \([1,T_{25}]\) minus the 10 elements of \(S_1\cup S_2\cup S_5\cup S_{10}\) that are at most \(T_{25}\). Counting gives \(T_{25}\ge 30\) when \(T_{10}\le T_{25}\), and a short check handles the other case, giving sum \(\ge 55\).
- \(x+y\ge 200\): if \(x\le y\), the 125 elements of the \(\{1,5,25,125\}\) blocks and the 25 elements of the \(\{2,10,50\}\) blocks all lie in \([1,y]\), so \(y\ge 150\) and \(x\ge 50\). If \(x>y\), a similar count gives \(x\ge150\), so \(x+y\ge 275\).

Hence the total is at least \(9+40+200+250=499\). The construction above attains it: \(1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499\).

VERDICT: REJECT
